title: I'm a teacher
goal: Use the verb *is* to state someone's job, nationality, and identity, and answer *is* questions with *Sea* and *Ní hea*.
bekal: tell when to use *is* and when to use *tá*
build *Is múinteoir mé* / *Ní múinteoir mé* / *An múinteoir tú?*

notes: **Is múinteoir mé — the second verb "to be", and a back-to-front word order.** Irish has two verbs for "to be". You've been using *tá* since Unit 1 for states. *Is* is for **identity** — job, nationality, name. The order is *Is* + what you are + who. So "I'm a teacher" comes out as *Is múinteoir mé* — literally "is teacher me". Never write *Tá mé múinteoir*.

**Sea and Ní hea — words that look like "yes" and "no", but only for is.** Questions starting with *An bhfuil …* are answered *Tá* or *Níl* (Unit 2). Questions starting with *An* + a noun — that is, *is* questions — are answered *Is ea* (often written and said *Sea*, SHAH) or *Ní hea* (nee HAH). Answering *Tá* to *An Sasanach tú?* is the classic beginner's mistake.

**Ní hea, Cé hé — the h that slips in before a vowel.** You've now seen this pattern several times: *go hiontach*, *a hocht*, and now *ní hea* and *cé hé*. A handful of small Irish words add an *h* to the next word if it starts with a vowel. It isn't séimhiú and it isn't urú — it's a third, lighter way of smoothing over two vowels meeting.

**Is é sin Liam — naming a specific person needs an extra word.** To classify ("he's a musician"), *Is ceoltóir é* is enough. But to equate two specific things ("that's Liam"), you need an extra pronoun after *is*: *Is **é** sin Liam*, *Is **í** sin Máire*. Use *é* for men and masculine things, *í* for women, *iad* for plurals.

sections.title: Is — the four forms you need

blocks.text: Notice that *is* never changes for different people. Only the pronoun at the end changes: *Is múinteoir mé / tú / é / í / muid / sibh / iad*.

blocks.title: Tá or Is — deciding in three seconds
items: If what follows is an **adjective** or a **place**, use *tá*: *Tá mé tuirseach*, *Tá mé sa bhaile*, *Tá mé go maith*.
If what follows is a **noun** saying *what* or *who* someone is, use *is*: *Is múinteoir mé*, *Is Éireannach í*, *Is mise Budi*.
Quick test: could it change tomorrow? "Tired" can change, so *tá*. "Indonesian" can't, so *is*.

One exception worth remembering: a **job seen as temporary** can use *tá … i mo …* — *Tá mé i mo mhúinteoir* ("I'm working as a teacher"). The difference is subtle, and *is* is always safe for beginners.

blocks.text: Notice the endings *-óir*, *-eoir* and *-aí*: all three make "doer" nouns, like English "-er". *Ceol* (music) → *ceoltóir* (musician). *Scríobh* (write) → *scríbhneoir* (writer). All these words are masculine, so *an múinteoir*, *an dochtúir*, with no séimhiú — even when the person is a woman.

blocks.title: Asking what someone does
items: *Cén obair atá agat?* (kyayn UH-bir uh-TAW AH-gut) — "what's your job?", literally "what work is at you?"
*Cad a dhéanann tú?* (kod uh YAY-nan too) — "what do you do?" This uses the present tense, which you'll learn in Unit 10.
The answer always uses *is*: *Is dochtúir mé*, *Is feirmeoir mé*. If you're not working: *Is mac léinn mé* or *Níl post agam faoi láthair* ("I don't have a job at the moment").

blocks.text: Irish nationality words end in *-ach*, and the same word works as both noun and adjective: *Is Éireannach é* ("he's Irish") and *ceol Éireannach* ("Irish music"). Notice that many country names carry the article *an* as part of the name — like English "the Netherlands".

blocks.title: Two names that trip people up
items: *Éire* is the country; *Gaeilge* is the language; *Éireannach* is the person. English uses "Irish" for two of these — Irish doesn't.
*Béarla* means "the English language" — and it's unrelated to *Sasana* (England). So an English person is a *Sasanach* (hence the Scottish "Sassenach"), but the language they speak is *Béarla*.
Other language names add *-is* or have their own form: *Fraincis* (French), *Gearmáinis* (German), *Spáinnis* (Spanish), *Sínis* (Chinese), *Indinéisis* (Indonesian).
